newsitem.title: INDIA: Four killed in Kashmir poll violence.
newsitem.headline: Four killed in Kashmir poll violence.

text.p: At least four people were killed in scattered violence and heavy cross-border shooting on Saturday during Kashmir's first local elections since a revolt against Indian rule erupted six years ago, authorities said.

Two brothers, aged 12 and 13, were killed in a mortar attack by suspected separatist militants in Tujjar village, 50 km (31 miles) northwest of Srinagar, summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, police said.
The boys had been playing in a field when the mortar shell exploded nearby. Police said seven other people were injured.
Indian authorities said a child was killed when Pakistani troops fired on Keran village on the state's northern border.
Indian and Pakistani troops exchanged fire in at least four places along their 830-km (520-mile) long Himalayan border, Indian defence officials said.
Cross-border shooting is common but an Indian army spokesman said the firing was heavier than usual and in more places.
"This is a quantum jump over routine border firing," he said.
The spokesman said Pakistani troops used heavy artillery, machine-guns and small guns. Apart from Indian security positions, they also targeted communication networks and roads.
"They are just trying to harass the people. It is not worrisome," he said.
One defence official said some rockets were fired at Indian positions from across the Pakistani border in Drass village on the Ladakhi plateau, in the state's eastern sector.
"We are unperturbed by their firing," he said, "But this is unusual in the Drass sector."
Pakistan and India have fought two of their three wars since independence in 1947 over the region. Pakistan controls one third of Kashmir and has staked a claim over the rest.
Meanwhile, a bystander was killed in cross-fire when militants and security forces clashed in Mard village, about 75 km (45 miles) southwest of Srinagar, police said.
Elsewhere in the mountainous state, two small bombs exploded but no one was injured. Police said a homemade bomb was defused in Baramulla town, 50 km (30 miles) northwest of Srinagar.

Since the outbreak of the rebellion in 1990, some 10 to 15 people on average have been killed each day in the state in clashes between security forces and militants, as well as in bomb, grenade and other attacks, according to police records.
About 200,000 soldiers, paramilitary troopers and police were deployed to prevent attacks on over 2,000 polling booths in 26 of the state's 87 constituencies voting on Saturday.
Voting in other constituencies will be over three days -- September 16, 21 and 30.
Authorities said turnout was mixed and generally lighter in the mostly Moslem Kashmir Valley than in the Hindu majority Jammu region in the south and in Buddhist Ladakh.
Few voters were seen at booths in Baramulla. But at nearby Pattan town hundreds of people queued to vote.
At least five leading separatists, including Shabir Shah, sometimes called "the Nelson Mandela of Kashmir", were detained or placed under house arrest, their aides said.

Most leading separatist groups have urged voters to boycott the polls, viewed as crucial to Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's efforts to restore democracy in the state, where more than 20,000 people have been killed since early 1990.
Voters in several localities said security personnel forced them to cast ballots. There were widespread allegations of coercion in a general election in May but officials denied the claims.
